title: Template release gate registry
description: The committed release decision `scripts/template/release-contract.ts` validates. This surface is TEMPLATE-ONLY and it is the only one in the program that is: it carries no capability, no fence, no `capabilitySignatures` entry, no `packageRules` entry, no residue token and no `ownershipRules` `copy` entry, and its workflow step lives inside a `template-only` block. The reason is measured rather than preferred — the gate reads `fixtures/template/*.toml`, `fixtures/golden/*.json` and this file, and all three are omitted from every render, so a rendered project would receive a command whose inputs are absent. That is the `dead command` `specs/template-capability-model/spec.md` forbids. The guard therefore asserts its own ABSENCE from all three fixtures rather than its presence. Nothing here is ever a query: a release decision is a DECLARATION checked against local Git objects and the tracked tree, never against a network the guard cannot reach and a Checks API a fine-grained token cannot read. And a record never upgrades a gate: this file may record an operator checkpoint, but that record grants no authority beyond the exact named scope.

decision.description: `candidate` while the tree is under review; `released` only after the runbook's post-merge steps have all happened. The pull request that introduces this file must ship `candidate`: a guard that read `released` from a tree whose tag does not exist would be a record upgrading its own gate.

auditedSource.description: The commit this declaration describes, pinned by both its own id and its tree id so a rewritten history cannot keep the pin. The guard resolves both through local Git objects and refuses a commit that is not an ancestor of HEAD.

release.description: The release artefact, which is one annotated Git tag on the merge commit and nothing else. There is no `version` field in `package.json` on purpose: that file renders into every downstream project, which would inherit a version from a template it did not write. `.template-ref` is already the mechanism a project uses to say which template it is on, and a tag is what it should point at.

plannedTag.description: The annotated tag the runbook creates on the merge commit. Declared rather than created here: the tag cannot exist until the merge commit does.

changelogHeading.description: The `CHANGES.md` heading that carries this release. The guard asserts the heading exists, so the tag and the changelog cannot disagree.

changeName.description: The OpenSpec change this release closes. It must still be ACTIVE while the pull request is open; archiving is a post-merge step.

templateRefMechanism.description: The existing `which template am I on` mechanism the tag is for.

goldens.description: The committed render expectations. A golden is a FULL manifest — path, mode and sha256 for every file of a render — because a structure-only expectation catches an added or a dropped file and nothing else, and the failure class that matters most is a renderer substitution that stops substituting: identical file list, different bytes. The counts cross-check themselves so a half-updated golden is a refusal rather than a smaller diff.

directory.description: Where the committed manifests live. Omitted from every render.

regenerateWith.description: The named command that rewrites the goldens. It is a command and never an environment variable: a golden regenerated as a side effect of the run that compares it is not an expectation.

totalFileCount.description: The sum of every fixture's `fileCount`. Declared separately so half-updating one golden fails instead of passing quietly.

manifest.description: The committed golden manifest for that fixture.

fileCount.description: How many files the render emits. Zero is a hard failure: a golden over nothing is an expectation nobody earned.

omittedCount.description: How many tracked template paths the render leaves out. It rises whenever a template-only artefact is added, which is exactly what this stage does.
